en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Recitation of Great Homage (A Prayer of Veneration to the Buddhas)
Thus: *ko*; *ne*, *saṃ*;
*satthā*, *nesaṃ*; *khemaṃ*, *dātā*;
*heḷāta-*, *kkāro* *so*; *jantūnaṃ*, *no mā nu*.
Thus, having destroyed the blindness of the world, he is the one who has slain the owl;
the awakener of the seed of beings,
the sun-like Victor who shatters the three realms of existence.
I shall dispel the great darkness by which the multitude of people,
seeing those who have sunk into the cycle of existence at the foot of the Conqueror, seek after false omniscience.
Having abandoned what is miserable and directed his aspiration toward liberation,
he who governed with compassion— to that Sage I pay homage.
My life, my wife, and even my wealth, I would now give up.
In the *Buddhinidāna*, this was told by the Sage concerning Cīna:
Having abandoned his body along with his kin, and having performed an excellent act of giving,
that bull among men fulfilled the noble virtue of supreme renunciation.
Having been King Nekkhamma, he [attained] Senabbidha as the best in wisdom;
Vedehinda attained Vīrukkaṃsa, and Khantīvādī attained patience as supreme.
He was Sutasoma, the Tathāgata, and Temiya attained the excellence of fortitude.

I pay homage to him who, having fulfilled the perfections— difficult indeed to perform in three ways, such as eating but one meal, the supreme loving-kindness, and equanimity even amidst hair-raising terrors—
attained the most excellent enlightenment, the essence of infinite Dhamma.
Having abandoned the wheel-turning monarch, who was brought down, crushed,
and accompanied by his army and mounts— the Wielder of the Thunderbolt defeated the Evil One;
let us bow to the Victor, the supreme bringer of victory and great benefactor.
I bow to him who, by means of his manifested forms, was gazed upon by witnesses;
who, while walking on the Cankama, severed the doubt of Māra; who performed miracles through supernormal power;
and who is possessed of the divine eye. I pay homage to that Visionary One.
I pay homage to that Abhidhamma, honored by gods and men, which the Buddha, generating immeasurable splendor, taught in the Jewel House (Ratanaghara) to Sīsupāla.
It is the Dhamma that arose near the Nigrodha tree, which even one who is not a master of learning can discern with ease.
I pay homage to that Sugata, the supreme leader, who attained the peerless enlightenment after overcoming great hardship;
he who was brought into solitude by Mucalinda,
the lord of nāgas, amidst all the clouds.
I pay homage to the Conqueror of Māra, of incomparable wisdom, who experienced that bliss of liberation and who,
as a compassionate one, dwelt in the royal palace.
O Bhoja, you who possess infinite virtues,
who are the source of the essence of enjoyment, whose dwelling is the Unconditioned,
I, being alone, pay homage to you, the Great Sage.
Having conquered again and again the banner of victory,
having won again and again the supreme drink of victory;
one should drink again and again, bowing with a well-discerned mind to that [Victor].
I considered what was to be understood with equanimity. Having conquered [the Māra],
the Victor spent seven days there,
and having shaken off [defilements], he went back again to Nigrodha.
Born for the sake of the well-expounded Dhamma,
with thoughts uplifted by the discourse on the Dhamma,
together with the hosts of Maruts and Brahmā—
When Ratnadāma Meru requested it,
the Ten-Powered One gave his promise to teach; I pay homage to him.
Having gone to the Isipatana forest,
the Teacher taught the Dhamma-wheel,
which is the manifestation of truth, at Migadāya.
First, the Sutta is of six kinds.
Having given his promise to the King of Magadha,
he then went to Rājagaha and instructed [the people].
To those beings afflicted by foul diseases and acute pain,
one should give that medicine and pay homage to the physician.
In Kapila, the abode of the Śākyas, there was a settlement.
Having shattered the banner of pride with the winds of diligence,
you caused the nectar of the Dhamma to be drunk by your father and his lineage;
I pay homage to the Lord of the Sakyas, the one who reveals the mind.
Having renounced boundless wealth,
he who was called Anāthapiṇḍika dwelt in the well-constructed monastery for the greater benefit of the multitude.
I pay homage to him who sounds the drum of the True Dhamma,
who is endowed with merit, possessed of excellent marks,
stainless, and shining like a blazing lamp.
I pay homage to the Sugata, who knows the island [of Nibbāna], who is free from affliction and blameless; the Sun-like Sage who,
with the radiance of the Dhamma, [illuminates] the people—
I pay homage to him who, like the sun, dispelled the dense darkness of delusion and ignorance through his noble heat; he who, red with compassion, attained perfect awakening,
and whose nature is cool yet radiant with the light of wisdom.
The Lord of Sages, who shines like the moon amidst the expanse of the sky with his host of stars,
surrounded by the assembly of Noble Ones throughout the three worlds— him [I honor].
He paid homage with deep reverence to the radiant splendor that had emerged.
The thirty perfections are its roots and sub-roots;
the branches and sub-branches are the middle and lower bodies of wisdom.
Whose eyes of the Buddha’s vision see what is favorable and unfavorable,
whose trunk of compassion discerns what is blooming and what is not,
and whose knowledge of the pith and the non-pith distinguishes the heartwood from the sapwood;
The sprouts are all-encompassing, the stalk is virtue;
the remaining qualities are the honey-filled fruits,
learning is the rind, and the characteristics are the sap.
May those gods who have attained long life, having conquered Māra,
honor the one born on earth as a Lamp-Maker,
who has set forth the infinite seed of skillfulness.
I pay homage to the Sage of the Single-Grown Tree,
who destroys the enemy— the Mara and the sectarians—
and dispels darkness while establishing the dharma of the city.
The gateway-tower is the hindrance to virtue;
the supreme and excellent watchtower is faith;
the well-disciplined gatekeepers are mindfulness; and the battlement is concentration.
The chariot of knowledge with its swift and powerful wheels,
the mansion and hall of the path of Dhamma, accompanied by its attendants,
and having the General of the Dhamma as its noble master.
The second [teacher] was Sutaparohita,
a supreme seer who possessed the great ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa),
a knower of the Vinaya, and a protector of the Dhamma.
In the lineage of Dhamma kings, which dispels the fear of existence,
every noble person and commoner has heard, again and again,
the measured and limited [teachings] that serve as a refuge for those whose virtues are infinite.
The offering made, the homage paid by beings bowing down—
may that auspiciousness in each existence flow forth for you.
May he who is delightful to the world, whose wisdom is charming, [be attained].
I bow to the one who has reached the end of the world,
who has transcended both fear and danger, the banner of the world who strikes down the banner of pride,
the one honored by the world, the supreme among those worthy of offerings.
The fruit of the crest-jewel, the adornment for the eyes,
the ornament for the ears, the ornament for the face,
the neck-ornament, success, and the nectar that delights the mind.
The *kiriyaññudara* is that which produces two moments of subsequent consciousness.
The waist-ornament (*kaṭivibhūsana*) is the middle [ornament] for women;
it is a fragrant ointment, a worn ornament, and a decoration.
I pay homage to the one Sage, the supreme among men,
who is clothed in the unsurpassed garment of the paṭakhilaññu tree;
he who possesses the excellent mindfulness, the pure speech, and the wisdom of the chief of the Ibbhas.
Suvīriya, Vasuvāha, Pītisela;
Gahapati, Samathagga, Thīpasaddhi;
Asaṇiya, Sunupekkha, and Sattabhoga.
The four bases of psychic power, with the divine ear as their companion,
are well-surrounded by stainless nobles;
they have a pure retinue and are pleasing to gods and men.
I pay homage to the Lord of the Wheel of the Ten Powers.
With concentration as the outer rim, mindfulness as the sixth mountain,
and energy as the fifth, with life-force in the middle and good karma—
The third is Suvācādutiya, the supreme Bhiseṭṭha,
and Samātakkapubba with Sattappavāra;
these produce the excellence of various kinds of knowledge and power.
The month of Māsa, possessing great majesty for the gods,
is delightful with the smoke and radiance of incense,
honoring the Sugata, the bull among men, the king of sages.
The ocean of the Dharma-jewel with its waters of virtue,
deep with the family-pillar of mindfulness and the waves of analytical knowledge,
possessing a vast expanse of wisdom and a heart as pure as the morning sun—
Supported by eight pillars, it is wondrous and without beams;
it has many rafters meeting at a single point, a single flavor,
difficult to construct, and not made of accumulated materials.
I pay homage to that very one of vast and pure merit,
the supreme among bipeds, the ocean of virtues, the excellent moon; who,
having exerted his bow of the perfections of virtue, [attained the goal].
Naḷa, Mati, Mana, Bāra, Jahammukha;
with the arrow of firm composure, well-aimed,
may he thoroughly remove the stain, as the single wind clears the sky.
That which I have proclaimed— the supreme path and the quiver,
my armor of the ornaments of Dhamma and my singular strength,
the net of infinite knowledge, and the mantra of the Girisela mountain—
I pay homage to the All-Knowing One, whose command is supernatural power.
With the rain of excellent vows, the faith that is like good seed, the pair of wisdom and means as the plow,
and shame and fear of wrongdoing as the plowshare and goad;
The cord of tranquility, the essence of mindfulness,
difficult to attain through vigor, rooted in truth,
the restraint of the womb, and the liberation of gentleness.
O Great Ploughman, pay homage to the Sugata, whose refuge must be returned to for the sake of what is to be attained,
and who possesses the fruit of the Deathless with its manifold flavors.
He who is the foremost of gods in the city of the Thirty-Three, seated upon his noble throne, taught the Dhamma that dispels the suffering of the gods— the progenitors and lords—
to them for three months, as if playing with a child.
In the region of Desesā, I bow to the unconquerable one of great renown, who illuminates manifold beauty;
he who possesses immeasurable virtues and dispels the darkness among the Kurus.
I pay homage to that Teacher who proclaims the foundations of mindfulness for those devoted to the beautiful, who carries away the doctrines of others,
who wears the bowl of serenity, and whose right mindfulness is full of affection.
Supremely radiant, with effort directed toward all things,
the maker of all light, the lamp of the sublime Dhamma—
this one, kindled by the Victor, I revere.
Free from the stains of existence, yet free from the stains of non-existence;
honored, yet beneficial to the mind; beneficial to the mind, yet honored;
bringing about both worldly existence and transcendence, yet transcending both existence and worldly power.
The virtue of the virtuous person is for the virtuous person who is also noble;
it is adorned with the staff of morality, possesses the excellent attainment of concentration,
and is brilliantly illuminated by splendor, reaching the pinnacle of infinite wisdom.
I pay homage to the Jewel of the Supreme True Dhamma, the banner of the three worlds, which is beautifully adorned with the consecration of the eyes;
it is measured by the method of discipline and the discipline that transcends the mind.
O Victorious One, victory, non-victory, and supreme victory—O you who are like a mountain!
O you who analyze and distribute! O you who do not partake, yet distribute and analyze the mind!
O you who are the unequal and the equal, the equal and the unequal—bow down before you!
The supreme delight that transcends death,
the quality of wisdom that has reached the state beyond states, free from "mine" and "I";
the accumulation of conditions that is without accumulation, the mind that is without craving.
With its parts well-fitted, its joints well-fastened, and steady,
the Teacher set out on the straight path toward the region of liberation in his excellent chariot-drawn by a noble steed, with wheels whose rims were of leather.
With the axle of the Dhamma heard, joined with the linchpin of mindfulness, and possessing the banner of miracles;
with well-restrained spokes and unshakable felloes.
He who has completely fulfilled the noble truths through higher knowledge,
who is adorned with skillfulness, whose hands are free from pride,
who does not seek out harshness, and who delights in well-guarded virtue.
With the swift speed of intelligence that follows after [the object], with the staff of confidence established in the knowledge of time, and with the sword of mindfulness,
he is a daughter of the Conqueror and a mare for the taming of the mind.
I pay homage to you, O Vinaya, peerless caravan leader! You who possess the fierce flames of concentration,
who are accompanied by the stinginess of mastery over others' domains, and who are the crocodile of the female titthiyas—
those with evil views, the blind, and those caught in the grip of the yoke.
In the midst of many, he who was desired as a jewel performed a miracle;
even Jayakketu bowed down before him near Kaṇṭamba.
His supreme lotus-feet, endowed with the marks of a wheel and the dust of the radiance of his nails—
The gods among gods always wore upon their excellent heads that garland which shone with ten fingers’ breadth of rays from the crest-jewel of Subhāsisiri;
who could ever grow weary of bowing to him, so delightful to the mind?
Even the Buddha alone might praise one endowed with the quality of self-effacement for as long as he lives;
let him say whatever else he wishes, but do not disparage such a person, O wise one.
For there is no blame whatsoever in that destruction [of defilements] whose praise is infinite.
I pay homage to that Omniscient One, the Lord of all beings, the Protector of many.
He whose feet are like the first lamp, whose two eyes are like birds, whose body is the Dhamma, whose trunk is wisdom;
he whose tip of the trunk is speech, whose crest is refuge, whose tail is the Path, and whose limbs are beautiful.
I pay homage to that Lord, the foremost among conquerors, who is adorned with the ornament of virtue, stainless, the abode of the seventy-three qualities,
the one who bestows the fruit of liberation, and the enjoyer of freedom. I bow to him who [crosses] the ocean of this miserable saṃsāra,
which is agitated by the waves of defilements and causes extreme terror.
May the Lord of the Ship, whose face is the shore of peace, who restrains those who have strayed from the path,
place the multitude of people desiring to cross over onto the single supreme path;
having placed them there, may he protect them, and I pay homage to him with incomparable devotion.
To him whose body shines with a face like a hundred lotuses,
who holds a torch of the True Dhamma adorned with the banner of supreme splendor,
and whose upward-radiating brilliance blazes forth from his crown— until this very day, [I pay homage].
I worship that Sage, the Bull of the Sakyas, who is like the full moon;
he bestows the destruction of the darkness of the seventh [existence], having disciplined those to be trained,
making the forest of mental cultivation dustless, performing what is difficult for the three worlds, and overcoming all beings.
I bow with reverence to the Buddha, who possesses a voice that captivates and removes pride,
who brings men and non-men under his sway, who dispels distress with respect, and who rains down the Dhamma for all beings— like a rain-cloud; he whose body is like a banyan tree,
whose hands and feet are soft, and whose shanks are like those of an antelope, endowed with a Brahma-like voice.
Furthermore, the Sugata has body-hairs that grow singly from each pore like the sheaths of a lotus; the Sugata has feet that are well-placed;
his body-hairs are soft, fine, and curling to the right;
moreover, the Sugata possesses the physical form of a Brahma, with deep blue eyes, long heels, delicate skin, and a head crowned by a protuberance.
With forty teeth, even and white, with broad shoulders and full arms,
his feet marked by wheels, his teeth without gaps, and his ankles like those of a conch;
standing, he does not stoop, and while bending, he does not touch his knees with his hands.
The Victor has a torso like a banyan tree, eyelashes like those of a young bull, and the front half of his body like that of a lion.
He is endowed with seven convexities, long fingers, and beautiful, single hairs growing from each pore.
The Sugata has teeth that are perfectly white, skin the color of gold, and blue hair on the crown of his head.
The Fully Enlightened One, with a broad tongue, a lion-like jaw, webbed feet and hands,
and a cranial protuberance on his head— I bow to that Great Sage endowed with such virtues.
With rounded, tapering, beautiful fingers, and high, glossy nails stained with blood.
His ankles are concealed, his feet are even, and his stride is like that of a lion, a bull, or a swan;
he walks turning to the right, with perfectly rounded knees free of sinews and beautiful;
his body is well-proportioned and full of auspicious marks, his navel is deep, and his skin is smooth and unblemished, turning to the right.
With arms as long and thick as an elephant’s trunk, with well-proportioned, smooth, and slightly curved upper lips,
and with a body pure and free from hair, beautiful and gradually tapering like a lotus stalk;
possessing the strength of ten million elephants, he was handsome with a high, golden nose.
With teeth, gums, and flesh that are pure, bright, and lustrous, he is the refuge of the world;
with eyes of pure clarity and rounded canine teeth, the Lord of gods and men has lips as red as blood;
with a long, beautiful face, the Sage possesses deep, straight, and most radiant lines upon his body.
He possesses a mass of light in a halo one fathom wide, the most excellent of men, with long, wide, and beautiful eyes;
his five sense-faculties are clear, his eyelashes are as lovely as those of a bull, and his tongue is soft, tender, and red.
He is gentle, serene, radiant, and delicate, with a body as pure as the ocean and endowed with immeasurable virtues.
The Victor’s hair is soft, curling to the right, resembling collyrium, dark blue, and delicate;
it is smooth, even, dark blue, unentangled, and beautiful in its formation.
He who possesses this glossy hair on his head is one who has perfected a hundred virtues.
His head is exceedingly beautiful, resembling a well-formed umbrella free from blemish;
his ears possess long radiance, and his forehead is of a pleasing shape, smooth, well-proportioned, and broad.
His eyebrows are thick and long, and his face is lovely and elongated; his body is fragrant, his hands and mouth are large, and his forehead is wide and splendidly expansive.
I pay homage to the Peerless One, who is equal to the unequalled, whose inhalations and exhalations are mindful,
and who is adorned with the Ketumālā garland. Since even the mere sound of the appearance of a Buddha is exceedingly difficult to encounter in the world,
those who desire the various kinds of welfare and happiness for themselves and others should strive [to hear it].
May the virtuous constantly and respectfully pay homage to the Sugata— the refuge for gods and men, the remover of obstacles, and the field of merit—
by means of the power of their swift prostrations preceded by praise for that most excellent field.
In this very existence, [may they attain] the goal of reaching the supreme field.
Afflicted by the calamities of fear of disease and the like, with his store of merit for enjoyments exhausted and lacking even slight happiness,
he will— in his final existence— attain the supreme enjoyments of gods and humans and the power of the ultimate goal,
becoming one of those destined for the threefold sublime enlightenment, because of what he has done according to his own aspiration.
By this merit, may I be one of subtle, swift intelligence, affectionate in speech, and amiable;
faithful, possessing virtuous friends, having gone for refuge, virtuous, and devoted to generosity;
possessed of shame and dread of blame, skillful, of unblemished conduct, steadfast, and truthful in speech.
One who possesses great learning, who distinguishes between things, who works for the welfare of both self and others, who is like a jackal’s cry [in discernment],
and who is formidable; long-lived, free from disease, born of a pure family, renowned, devoted to the Dhamma,
detached, ever-steadfast, grateful, exceedingly gentle and upright in mind, and one who understands goodness and such virtues.
"May I live by the Dhamma, delighting in much wholesome conduct, with little anger and free from greed;
and may I perform other such deeds, making this aspiration in my final existence so that I may partake in liberation and Nibbāna.
Thus spoke Buddhaghosa, even while his body was wasting away.
One should give what is to be given, having abandoned what is to be abandoned, exactly as it ought to be done.
One should repeatedly abandon even something of great value and ancient,
as well as that which is difficult to restrain— namely, the transgression of sensual desires— for the sake of giving elsewhere.
(3) This new homage has been performed by me, who am a novice, out of reverence for the Teacher,
with the purpose of establishing the experience of what has been heard.
(4) From verses of a single syllable up to those of twenty-six syllables—
There are seventy-five [verses] on birth, and eighty-four on the conditioned.
This [work] is composed with eight [verses] more, including the sections on the yojana and so forth.
May those sensual pleasures that possess the meanings as they have been described always sustain you.
To him who is more enchanting than the king of kings,
who bears a flood of qualities surpassing those of the god of gods,
who is a Brahmā beyond Brahmā, and who has reached the end of all existence—
I pay homage to the one whose saṅghāṭī robe is a cry of victory,
who is stainless and yet the very essence of form, the god of gods among men,
who is immovable and yet the refuge for those in fear.
I bow to the Mother of the Sage, the joy of the joyless,
the protector of the protectorless,
who brings an end to the cycle of existence. That sage, whose copper-red nails are elevated and whose ten fingers are perfectly round and beautiful—
He has legs like those of a lion, a bull, or a swan; his ankles are hidden and his body and face are well-proportioned.
His hair is soft, delicate, and fine; his body is pure, stainless, and radiant.
His eyes are endowed with the five kinds of grace, and he possesses a fragrant mouth and a prominent nose.
Possessing the strength of a thousand million elephants, with lips of beautiful red, well-rounded teeth,
long and straight eyebrows, and a tongue that is soft, thin, and red;
with a head of radiant beauty like a parasol, adorned with excellent hair like a crest-ornament.
I bow my head in homage to the most excellent Lord of Sages, endowed with such secondary marks.
That Sage is far removed from all defilements because he has destroyed the enemies of defilement;
that Best of Men is honored by the three worlds, including the gods and non-gods alike.
The Sage is one who has fully realized the infinite objects of knowledge worthy of being known;
he is endowed with conduct, possesses the threefold supernormal knowledge, and is well-spoken among people, thus he is the Sugata.
He is the knower of the world, because of his thorough understanding of the world; he is the incomparable tamer of men.
The Charioteer, the Victor, the follower of his own instruction, the Caravan-leader who ferries beings across the difficult path;
he awakens to the Four Truths in their entirety by himself and causes the multitude of living beings to awaken—thus he is called the Buddha.
He is like a lotus flower suffused with the light of the sun, and he is fully blossomed through the knowledge of the Path.

He is the Blessed One because he has abandoned the defilements (bhagga-kilesa); he is the one who has cast out the three states of existence (tibhava-vamita-gamana) because he is a vessel for the noble ones;
he is "Bhaga" because he honors the sixfold division of the essence of the True Dharma as it has been analyzed;
and he is "Sujana" because he possesses a splendor of glory and radiance that is peerless among the assembly of beings and immeasurable in its virtuous qualities.
The appearance of a Buddha is the sole foundation for the gods and humans, the peerless object of true praise, and the supreme refuge.
O you of beautiful voice, what more difficult than this could possibly exist in this world?
Therefore, those who are virtuous and aspire to the Omniscient One—who possesses manifold benefits, happiness, and unsurpassed glory—should pay him homage.
By this merit, these beings will be free from fear, calamity, and oppression in this visible world, and in the hereafter they will both be auspicious and pure;
having experienced infinite, unimpeded glory and splendor of happiness, they will become partakers of the unsurpassed state.
He is endowed with wheels on his feet, with soft hands and feet, and with well-planted feet.
The Buddha has shanks like those of the eṇī deer, skin with the luster of gold, and long heels, O Protector.
His private parts are concealed in a sheath, his skin is exceedingly smooth,
and beneath his webbed feet he possesses high-arched insteps, deep blue eyes, and long-fingered hands.
Standing yet not stooping, with arms reaching both knees when unextended, his body hair grows singly from each pore,
his teeth are even and forty in number, and his body hair points upward like collyrium;
his torso is as broad as his shoulders, his jaw is unhindering, and he possesses the seven protuberances.
With a jaw like a banyan tree or a paribimba fruit, with shoulders like those of a lion,
he has a full set of forty teeth, well-aligned and white, with beautiful, pure fangs;
his hair is soft and fine, and his neck is even, round, and fleshy.
The Lord of Sages, whose voice is like Brahmā’s, who again speaks with a gentle smile,
his head adorned with a protuberance, the Eldest of the World, beautified by the thirty-two marks and easy to endure—
I bow to him. The Great Prostration is concluded.
The Praise of the Tigumbacetiya.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
He who, at the foot of Dīpaṅkara, renounced the footprint that had come into his hand;
I revere the hair-tuft of him who, desiring perfect enlightenment,
fulfilled the great requisites for awakening and attained the unsurpassed state. (Pathyāvattagāthā)
He attained Buddhahood; I pay homage to his excellent hair-relic.
(The Pathyāvatta Verse) Having attained Buddhahood, he proclaimed it after passing beyond six places.
I bow to his excellent hair at the Sanctuary of Liberation.
(This is a *pathyāvatta* verse with the *vipulā* meters on the letters *ra* and *bha*).
Therein, even the *sakkadattiya* offering, the *nāgalatā*, and the *harītakī*;
He consumed the water of Lake Anotatta; I revere his crown-lock of hair.
(A *rakāra-vipulā* *pathyāvatta* verse.
At that time, the bowl from Mount Muggasela was presented by the Great Kings.
The Tathāgata accepted it; I pay homage to that head-offering.
(This is a *rakāra-vipulā* verse in the *pathyāvatta* meter.
At that time, from the two brothers, [the Buddha received] a ball of honey.
He even partook of the flour-mash; I bow to his glorious head.
(This is a *pathyāvatta* verse in the *takāravipulā* meter.
To Tapussa and Bhallika, he then gave the two-fold refuge.
I bow first of all in the world to him who bears glory.
(This is a verse with the *vipulā-pathyā-vatta* meter containing the letters *ra* and *na*).
At that time, he gave eight hairs to those who were standing there attending him.
I bow to that Protector who, looking out for the welfare of the world,
[acted thus]. Having brought even them [the kings] to Pokkharabbati, they did [this] for you.
This is the Sajīvakesa Cetiya, the very first of all [shrines].
It releases blue rays on every Uposatha day. (A Pathyāvatta verse in the Makāra-vipulā meter).
I always bow to that Blessed One who acts for the welfare of the world.
(This is a *rakāra-vipulā* *pathyāvatta* verse.
At the time when he was a Bodhisatta, [he built] the Cūḷāmaṇi and Dussacetiya.
At the time of the Buddha, I bow down to this very first one.
(A *rakāra-vipulā* *pathyāvatta* verse.
I bow down, I pay homage, I worship the hair-tuft upon his head.
May this merit be for me a condition for the destruction of the taints.
(This is a Pathyāvatta-gāthā with the *takāra* and *nakāra* vipulās.
The recitation at the Tigumbacetiya is finished.
Vāsamālinī:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Though you are aged among the Conquerors, you are a Buddha, one who possesses true knowledge.
"I shall not rise up before you; I am building a celestial mansion.
(The Stanza on the Slender Waist) "To the shore of Mahāsamata, which receives the supreme worship of men;"
Just as a golden image [is seen] when the light is full, so too [is seen] the Well-Awakened One,
the Bull among Men, the Physician for the World. (In the Kumāralalitā metre) He who is the Bull among Men, the Well-Awakened One, the Physician for the World.
We pay homage with zeal to the one who has compassion as his natural disposition.
(In the Kumāralalitā meter:
One of virtuous conduct brings about welfare and rejoices in the midst of happiness.
Know him as the Awakened One, the Conqueror who has reached the end of suffering.

He is the kinsman whose defilements have been extinguished, he who shines with the radiance of gold. (In Kumāralalita verse) He is the kinsman, free from all taints, who possesses the luster of the color of gold.
To him of the Gotama clan, who is empty [of self], homage to that Lion among Men!
(In the Citrapadā meter) To the Buddha, pure, sought after by the world, a lamp, yoked to yoga, I bow.
Having transcended the flood, he does not sink; he is one who causes others to revere and one who dispels their sorrows.
(From the *Vijjummālāgāthā*) He is possessed of wealth, a protector, cool with compassion, and a friend to the world.
In the three realms, fame indeed belongs to that giver, and it shall belong to me as well.
(The Student’s Verses) He is honored, though he may be harsh-spoken; he is like a kinsman, beautiful, and happy.
The Dharma is known, and homage is paid to him whose very qualities have been praised.
(The Samānikā Verse) Victory is the banner established among the people, abiding playfully in great bliss.
I bow to the Auspicious One, who is radiant and luminous; may He grant me welfare and happiness.
(The *Pamāṇikā* verse) May there be auspiciousness born of full merit, possessing the quality of praise from one's own kin and relatives.
To the Victor Vimala, who has severed the terrors [of existence] and whose feet walk upon the ground of wisdom— (the Halamukhī verse)—
[he is] mindfulness, intelligence, purity, radiance, praise, the sage, and a blissful body.
The Lord, the son of Manujapuma, the supreme victor, the giver of peace;
he who is the Buddha, the most excellent one, acting with grace toward the world. (Bhujagasusugāthā)
Transcending the world, fearless, established in bliss;
having crossed over, the peerless one who bears the welfare of others—
I bow to the Lord of Sages, the stainless Conqueror.
(Suddhavirājitagāthā) To the Lord of Devas,
the preeminent Chief of the Assembly, the ultimate goal,
the cessation of becoming and birth, Nirvana;
I pay homage to this beautiful golden face,
which is stainless and has shaken off the dust of conflict.
(The Paṇava Verse)
Known as the banner of the Gotama clan,
born like Mount Meru in the field of the world,
he who crushed Māra at the foremost spot on the sacrificial ground.
O wise one, speak among the learned;
I pay homage to the Lord who is served by those who possess wisdom.
(The Rummavatī Verses)
The Buddha is pure, possessing immeasurable virtues;
disciplined, liberated, and free from darkness like the moon;
he is like the sun whose brilliance shines in the sky.
Fruitful is your salutation. (The Mattāgāthā) He who has conquered all,
having indeed vanquished Māra—
He who has mastered the essence of the teachings,
who is filled with accumulated merit,
bows to that wise one who is blossomed with intelligence.
(Campakamālāgāthā) O one of golden form, worthy of comparison,
preeminent hero, honored and served!
I bow down to that place, the realm of the lotus-born,
where gods and humans alike pay homage.
(From the *Manoramāgāthā*)
He went twice to the Gata mountain,
and he practiced meditation on the moving rock known as Seleya;
he spent three years on the high plateau.
I bow to the Buddha who has passed away.
(The Ubbhāsakantagāthā) O monks,
listen to the young, the commoner, and the elder.
Having spoken thus— subtle, straight, and true—
I bow to that which is described as divine, consisting of ritual action,
powerful, honored, and proclaimed.
(Upaṭṭhitagāthā) 20. O Siddhattha,
you who dwell in the city protected by the most excellent and divine beings,
you have emerged from the elements.
The Buddha was honored by the hosts of Māra in Saṅkassa;
elsewhere, I am unable to perform such worship.
(Indavajirā Gāthā)
He who offered a beautiful, praised, and silver yoke for the sake of power— what was the purpose of that golden,
piled-up, fixed, red, and pleasing gift?
I bow to him who has gone to Līlā, who is gentle and whose lute is joyful and harmonious.
(In Upendravajrā meter) He who has sacrificed, being full of joy and friendliness...
It is very pleasant, firm, supple, and well-proportioned;
it is established, bounded, smooth, and broad—
I bow to that which is worn away, subtle, and soft.
(Sumukhīgāthā) Having taken up the bowl, he awakened the people of the Soga region;
having understood the meaning, he descended at Sonama.
The Lord of the Earth honored the Śākya lineage and proclaimed the Dharma that is free from acquisitions and worldly attachments.
(In Dodhaka meter)
When I had requested these four things and they were granted to me,
I obtained the wealth I desired and crossed over the flood;
having performed that service, I bow to him who is adorned with the yellow robe.
In this world, O Lord, that indeed is a thorn.
(From the *Sālinī-gāthā*) The world of beings is like a river that carries away the banner.
There, Aggavaṃsa, Rājavallabha, Muddhamanta,
Bhaddasela, Soka, Pacitabhatta, Pabuddha, Saddhāyoga,
Bhajita, Soṇa, and Muccaka— these were the teachers.
(Vātompī Gāthā) For the Victors who stand above all known forms,
even a hair-tip becomes vast.
"He is known as Deva Suyāma, the Conqueror;
therefore, O happy one, we now bow down to him.
(Sirīgāthā)
Puṇṇaka, Kusuma, and Sevana served him;
like elephants trumpeting as they ascend into the sky, Sundara and Nami likewise honored him;
by him, may there be victory for me.
Indeed, one who gives land that produces the luster of merit—
when the mother's lifespan has been exhausted here in the past—
To those who were virtuous, well-born, and pure in conduct,
adorned with gold like wind-shaken palm trees— those thirty-three mothers,
I worship you, calling out, "Father! Father!"
(Svāgatagāthā) Above, the lotus-born one shines,
offering oblations, illuminated by white light.
I hear that the Lord of the World has washed away the stains from my feet,
having liberated me through the awakening of his mind.
(The Bhaddikā Gāthā)
O Sage, you who dwell in the forest, you who regard discipline with equanimity;
you who stand firm amidst the dead, O bird-like one, well-restrained;
you who have cast away the abyss of suffering and crossed over the agitation of the world.
Fearing his own name, I sought the austere enlightenment;
he who attended upon the pride of birth was one who hung low. (The Vaṃsaṭṭha Gāthā)
With harsh words from many worlds, you spoke ill of the wise man;
yet you abandoned even the root of views,
and with all your attainments, you bowed to what was desired.
(Indavaṃsāgāthā) In Verañjā,
the most excellent city, beautifully adorned,
in the Dūma Grove at Nelañjana, resounding with birds;
"Khemaṅkarā, Thūlatarā, Vidū, Sitā;
Et-aṅgamā, Pūnā, Namā, Virūpī.
(Indavaṃsāgāthā)
Even now, that son of Sārī attends upon him who is stainless;
though he has passed away, he brings that very method from wherever it may be.
Out of compassion, the Buddha indeed requested the discipline.
I bow even with great reverence to him who has well-conquered the mind;
that sage dwells like a river in the forest among the people. (A Toṭaka verse)
Vasabha, Udita, and Pariyanta are from the Gotama lineage;
Guṇika was named Gamiya; Nāgadāsa was Jutindhara; and Ghaṭita was Satha.
(Dūtavilambita-gāthā) While the Blessed One was seated in his small hut,
and Dhanavatī in her very spacious house, who was the lord of men?
When the sage obtained the pair [of garments],
he was soiled by the dust of the sun’s rays as his hair was being cut.
(Introductory Verse)

May all that has been done for my sake be established for the benefit and happiness of one who trains here in the first [stage]; having proclaimed it for the sake of destroying the craving of the greedy,
[may it lead to] the exhaustion of dryness.
And I pay homage to the pinnacle of what must be done.
(The Flower-Variegated Stanza) You,
O lofty one, shone with smoke in playful grace.
Though the tree stood firm against those who sought to uproot it,
and though he was greedy for them even when they were full, the Victor made [them his own];
I worship the Buddha, the benefactor of the world.
(Bhujaṅgappayātagāthā) To the Noble One among men,
the Ten-Powered One, the Widely Renowned, the Supreme Sage,
who dwells in the hut-like path of the noble ones;
He who has indeed abandoned talk concerning the ascetic practices and purity— him,
truly, one should honor here as the third [type of person].
(The Piyaṃvadā verses)
While dwelling in Vesālī, he established the fourfold assembly;
among them, he obtained those who were free from desire for gain and honor;
among the village folk, he enjoyed peace and tranquility.
"Even more than these, Suppiya spoke harsh words to Nami,
who was like a kāsū flower; therefore— " (from the *Lalitāgāthā*).
The wise man who speaks of virtues as they truly are follows the path of the virtuous;
he who walks the difficult road bows down to the excellent enlightened one.
(Pamitakkharāgāthā) At that time, the stainless and gentle Brahmā,
who delights in the company of young women, approached.
The virtues spoken of by one who dwells alone and remains steadfast—
these I bow to in the dust at the feet of the Victor.
(Ujjalāgāthā)
Knowing that he bestowed the *adhimutta* upon all,
the Elder Ānanda is recognized for the *coḷisutta*;
having performed the worldly [rites] in the presence of the body...
I pay homage to the compassionate one who dwells in the foremost state.
(The Vessadevī verse) Furthermore,
there is the well-spoken [teaching] on the intermediate morality.
In this world, one who has accumulated merit through long practice, who has awakened to the supreme state like a roasted fish,
and who is pure, having abandoned all worldly desires—
such a person is truly well-named as one who has gone forth into homelessness.
(Mālatī-gāthā) O beloved,
you have spoken of great virtue;
O Brahman, you are dear and pleasing to me.
I bow indeed to you, O Ambā, the supreme scholar, who once spoke even harsh words to me when I was exhausted.
(Kamalāgāthā)
When delusion is conquered, victory is won for the first time;
dwell in this delightful grove of Isipatana.
While all worldly activities are shaken, speak only of the sublime play.
I bow to the Victors who subdue even the terrible.
(The Pahāsinī Gāthā) May the city of Bajanagara dwell in prosperity for a thousand years.
I bow to this supreme among men, who brings welfare, who stands amidst the multitude of people at night as if they were dead,
who is the knower, free from tangles, and white in the forest.
O people, having composed this verse without gaps,
look at the third and fourth syllables yourself.
I bow down to him who has made his assembly free from agitation and impurity through his supreme authority,
and who has cast out all other states of existence.
(The Parājitā-gāthā)
While he was dwelling there in the city of Majjhimā,
at the great Maṇika Sakuṇakujavana grove,
he lived as one who carries the vehicle of welfare and peace.
"O Sage, drink this water which is cool on both sides.
(The Paharaṇakalikā Gāthā) Thus, in the sixth year, he dwelt there in that forest.
One should perceive all this as a mountain of filth;
having abandoned it, O man, one should seek a good destination for the sake of the ultimate goal.
One should bow to the food received, eat lightly, and shake off that which is harmful.
Surely you dwell here now,
and again there beyond, in the unconquered city of the Thirty-three,
great with the qualities of happiness.
The praise of the pair is not false nor is it vain;
I consider that praise to be like the peak of Mount Sineru compared to a mustard seed.
(Sasikalāgāthā)
The Lord of the Jinas dwells in the Bhesakaḷā Grove,
that abode of bliss for those of vast knowledge; he whose body is stainless, pure,
and upright, and who has brought an end to all suffering and fever.
I bow down to him who has abandoned even his delicate body on all sides.
(Mālinī verse) In that great, beautiful, and cool place,
He dwelt in Kusambī for nine years and more;
having abandoned the final suffering here, he indeed attained the ultimate bliss.
I pay homage to him who dispelled all that is base within the entire domain of the Teacher’s dispensation.
(Pabhaddaka Verses) Having abandoned the Naga in the Pālileyyaka forest, Yudhavatī waited upon the Naga-king;
having abandoned her foolishness, she stood there like a queen.
Then she dwelt among those who dwell in bliss, both in body and mind;
she was endowed with mindfulness, well-restrained, and had driven away Māra.
(Vāṇinīgāthā)
In this [work], there are ten chapters, including the "Bird's Abode" (*Dvijagāma*);
it contains more than one hundred and fifty verses composed in the *Hitopadeśa* style,
and it stands even during the month of Māgha with its various contrary meanings.
Even this [residence] at Pihavāsa was for the sake of separation from her;
thus, two more than ten—that is, twelve—were spent thereafter in Verañjā. (A Sikharaṇī verse) Then, beyond that, the tenth [residence].
I dwelt in the blue forest, causing great distress to the birds;
I have indeed grown weary here among these delightful creatures.
I bow to the one who bestows freedom from sorrow, the wise creator within the stainless flock of deer.
(Hiriṇīgāthā) He who dwells in splendor upon a mountain with its full upper slopes, amidst blooming flowers,
and surrounded by other desirable and immeasurable things;
Even in a dwelling constructed at Sāvatthī on the fourteenth day,
fear arises for one who has not cut off desire, even toward kinsmen, through the gateways [of the senses]. (Mandākantā-gāthā)
Sakka, having made Kappila subject, was the subduer of the Madakas;
Dakkha, dwelling among the Kappiyas, became a powerful lord over the Yamakas and others;
the Yakkha, having tamed Dabbika in the city of Soḷasa, [subdued] even Vaṅka.
When the supreme one had struck the drum that awakens the mind,
[the city] was filled with the fragrance of jasmine;
(in this *kusumitalatāvellita* meter) those who, having obtained their desires, frequented the royal palace from all ten directions.
Leaving his dwelling on the bank while tending the herd of cattle,
he went to the mountain slope; there, amidst the trees, he remained delighting in the movement [of meditation],
bestowing that state upon himself, endowed with virtue, like a young elephant here enduring physical fatigue.
(Verse on the Dispelling of Clouds) If one enjoys even a small portion of that which is beneficial— just as a drop from a cloud—
then how much more so should one dwell in the practice frequented by the wise?
When one's own village is ruined and another city is filled with enemies,
when one's home is seized and one's very roots are destroyed, even if one has conquered,
it is truly lost. (Saddūlavikkīlita verse)
In the five-and-five *mākara* [periods], and even beyond that with alms-food in the Jeta Grove,
he who sat there with mutual respect measured them out; in the Pubbārāma and Pubbavasiṭṭhārāma,
he applied himself to the *pāsika* [meditation] for a period of residence.
With a mind that is pure, stainless, and well-refined, one should pay homage. By this merit,
may I traverse the cycle of existence free from acquisitions and serve the truly noble ones.
May what has been given be well-grasped, surrounded by a pure assembly, and may I be free from disease;
may I have long life, great wisdom, and the easy acquisition of fame and wealth, and may I have virtuous friends;
and may I attain the supramundane path, accompanied by an even-minded retinue, reaching Nibbāna.
(Saddharāgāthā) Ka.
When three hundred and ninety-six years have passed in the Kaliyuga, the Teaching shall perish.
When the entire kingdom was thrown into turmoil by more than one thousand four hundred and twenty [rebels],
the city then became a heap of ashes due to the fighting between the brothers;
the community of monks fell into suffering from great slaughter and even met their end within the baskets [of the scriptures].
(Bhaddakagāthā) Kha.
Even if scattered among the shrines, he does not perish; he remains steadfast together with his retinue.
Having abandoned the various northern forests, he dwelt at the village of Kumbhakāra.
There, the people, in groups of hundreds, said to him: "Sir, please stay here; we shall serve all those who practice asceticism.
Having investigated whether it would be comfortable there, he indeed stayed for some days.

(Lalitagāthā) Ga. Therein, he who delights in the forest, who is well-conducted, who honors the True Dharma, and who is well-heard by those possessing the three knowledges— [he is] the one with the triple staff.
Well-yoked to his burden, well-born, and well-established, he traversed the marshy forests of the Kunadī river;
he gave that city to his ministers and placed his own treasury to the east.
When he was dwelling here, he was pure and possessed great splendor, even while seeking the requisites for his journey.
(Tanugāthā) Gha.
Composed on the sixth day of the month of Phagguṇa, this supreme work has reached its conclusion.
May this love indeed be fulfilled; may the virtuous deity protect it, or may it increase in the word of the Conqueror.
*Vāsamālinī* is finished.
